summary: Updates the ASN.1 modules for Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS) and related S/MIME formats from the 1988 to the 2002 version of ASN.1. There are no changes to the bits on the wire, only to the description syntax. It is informational.

eli5.summary: Rewriting a recipe in modern language without changing the dish. The messages look the same on the wire, but the description uses newer notation.

questions: what is the difference between asn.1 1988 and 2002
does rfc 5911 change the cms wire format
subtitle: The same CMS and S/MIME formats on the wire, with their ASN.1 descriptions rewritten in the 2002 version of the notation.

tldr.problem: The Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS) and related formats were described in ASN.1 modules written to the 1988 version of ASN.1, which has been deprecated, while some developers want the IETF to use the latest version.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 5911 republishes the ASN.1 modules from ten earlier RFCs, plus a new common AlgorithmInformation module, in the 2002 syntax, replacing the old ANY holes with objects and object classes.
tldr.outcome: There are no bits-on-the-wire changes to any format, only a change of syntax. The RFC is informational and is updated by RFC 6268.

today: RFC 5911 is an Informational RFC and is updated by RFC 6268. It has not been obsoleted. Its modules refer to RFC 3852 for the main CMS definitions, and the RFC itself notes that some references in its comments may already have been superseded by later RFCs.

sections.title: Why Rewrite the Modules
sections.content:
The Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS) and many associated formats are expressed in ASN.1, a notation for describing data structures. Most security-related RFCs, particularly those for PKIX, CMS and S/MIME, still used ASN.1 from the 1988 standard, which has been deprecated. Some developers would like the IETF to use the latest version.

RFC 5911 therefore updates a set of ASN.1 modules to conform to the 2002 version of ASN.1. Not every module is changed in substance; some are included just to make the set complete.
sections.eli5: The old description was written in an old-fashioned way of writing. This RFC says the same thing in the newer way people prefer.

sections.title: The Modules Included
sections.content:
Section 2 is a new common module, AlgorithmInformation, that does not come from any existing RFC. Sections 3 to 12 each hold the module from one earlier RFC: CMS Algorithms (RFC 3370), AES in CMS (RFC 3565), S/MIME 3.1 (RFC 3851), the main CMS module (RFC 3852), firmware package protection (RFC 4108), Evidence Record Syntax (RFC 4998), Enhanced Security Services (RFC 5035), authenticated-enveloped data (RFC 5083), AES-CCM and AES-GCM (RFC 5084) and CMS symmetric key management (RFC 5275).

Some modules get definitions from different places than the originals. The idea is that these modules, combined with those in RFC 5912, stand on their own and need not import from anywhere else. The comments inside the modules still point to the original RFCs, and some of those references may since have been superseded by later RFCs.
sections.eli5: It is a binder with ten rewritten chapters and one new shared page at the front that every chapter uses.

sections.title: Objects Instead of ANY Holes
sections.content:
The modules lean heavily on the object model of the 2002 ASN.1 documents. Places where 1988 syntax had ANY holes to allow variable syntax now use objects. Each algorithm type gets an object class, such as DIGEST-ALGORITHM, SIGNATURE-ALGORITHM, KEY-TRANSPORT, KEY-AGREE, KEY-WRAP, KEY-DERIVATION, MAC-ALGORITHM and CONTENT-ENCRYPTION, defined in the AlgorithmInformation module.

A set of short name prefixes makes the type of an object clear at a glance, so the same back half of a name can serve different objects. For example, id-sha1 is the object identifier while mda-sha1 is the message digest object for the same algorithm. Each module also defines object sets with consistent names, such as PublicKeys, and an importing module tells same-named sets apart by qualifying them with the module name.
sections.eli5: Instead of a blank box labelled 'anything goes', each algorithm now gets its own labelled box with rules for what fits inside.

sections.title: No Change on the Wire
sections.content: The central promise is that there are no bits-on-the-wire changes to any of the formats. This is purely a change to the syntax used to describe them, so an implementation that encodes and decodes CMS and S/MIME messages the old way produces and accepts the same bytes as one built from the new modules.
sections.eli5: The letters in the envelope are the same. Only the instructions for how to write them down have changed.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: Even though all the RFCs covered are security-related, the document itself has no security considerations. The ASN.1 modules keep the same bits-on-the-wire as the modules they replace.
sections.eli5: Because nothing about the messages changed, nothing about how safe they are changed either.
